```{python}
#| label: setup
#| code-summary: "Setup"
import duckdb
import polars as pl
from IPython.display import Markdown

from mf_scorecard import viz
from mf_scorecard.config import load_config, repo_path
from mf_scorecard.data.snapshots import SNAPSHOTS_TABLE

cfg = load_config()
con = duckdb.connect(str(repo_path(cfg["data"]["database"])), read_only=True)
eligible = f"FROM {SNAPSHOTS_TABLE} WHERE exclusion_reason IS NULL"

n_train_defaults = con.sql(
    f"SELECT count(*) FILTER (default_12m) {eligible} AND sample = 'train'"
).fetchall()[0][0]
yearly = con.sql(
    f"""SELECT snapshot_year,
        100 * avg(default_12m::INT) AS rate,
        100 * avg((default_12m AND NOT covid_forbearance)::INT) AS rate_ex_covid
    {eligible} GROUP BY 1"""
).pl()
ltv_dscr = con.sql(
    f"""SELECT
        CASE WHEN underwritten_dscr < 1.25 THEN 'Below 1.25x'
             WHEN underwritten_dscr < 1.5 THEN '1.25x–1.50x'
             WHEN underwritten_dscr < 2 THEN '1.50x–2.00x'
             ELSE '2.00x and above' END AS dscr,
        CASE WHEN loan_acquisition_ltv < 55 THEN 'Below 55%'
             WHEN loan_acquisition_ltv < 70 THEN '55%–70%'
             ELSE '70% and above' END AS ltv,
        min(underwritten_dscr) AS dscr_order,
        count(*) AS n,
        100 * avg((default_12m AND NOT covid_forbearance)::INT) AS rate
    {eligible} AND loan_payment_status = 'Current'
        AND underwritten_dscr IS NOT NULL AND loan_acquisition_ltv IS NOT NULL
    GROUP BY ALL"""
).pl()
```

SR 11-7 asks that a model's design be "generally supported by published
research and sound industry practice", that its methods be "explained in
detail with particular attention to merits and limitations", and that
developers compare the chosen approach with alternatives (p. 6). This
chapter sets out what the model has to do, what theory says drives
multifamily default, the methods considered, and the one chosen.

## What the model has to do

The model's job follows from its purpose (a rating scorecard) and from the
data built in the previous chapter:

- **Output.** A one-year, through-the-cycle probability of default (PD) for
  each performing loan, which maps to one of the performing grades of the
  rating scale (next chapter).
- **Ranking and calibration.** It must rank loans by risk, and its PDs must
  match observed default rates on average over the cycle.
- **Explainability.** Credit officers must be able to see why a loan got its
  grade and challenge it. Each input's effect on the PD should be visible
  and make economic sense.
- **Stability.** A loan's grade should change because its risk changed, not
  because of noise in the model.
- **Little data.** The training sample has `{python} f"{n_train_defaults:,}"`
  defaults. That is plenty for a handful of well-chosen drivers but not for
  many interactions.
- **Implementable.** The inputs must be ones a bank would have for its own
  loans at each review date.

## What drives multifamily default

The research on commercial and multifamily mortgages gives two economic
triggers for default:

- **Equity.** A borrower whose property is worth less than the loan has an
  incentive to stop paying, as in option-pricing models of commercial
  mortgages [@titman1989]. Loan-to-value (LTV) measures how far the property
  value can fall before this happens.
- **Cash flow.** A property whose net income does not cover the debt
  payment cannot pay without new money from the borrower. The debt service
  coverage ratio (DSCR) measures the cushion.

Default is most likely when both happen at once: the property no longer
covers its payments, and the owner has no equity to protect by putting more
money in. This **double-trigger** view is the standard model of multifamily
default [@goldberg2002]. Empirical work also finds that LTV and DSCR *at
origination* predict default less well than this theory suggests, because
lenders underwrite riskier properties to stricter LTV and DSCR limits, so
property and location characteristics carry much of the signal
[@archer2002].

Both points show up in the data. Among current loans, the one-year default
rate rises as acquisition DSCR falls and LTV rises, about
`{python} f"{ltv_dscr['rate'].max() / ltv_dscr['rate'].min():.0f}"` times
higher in the worst cell than in the best:

```{python}
#| label: tbl-ltv-dscr
#| tbl-cap: "One-year default rate (%, excluding COVID forbearance) of current loans by acquisition DSCR and LTV. Observations in parentheses."
cells = ltv_dscr.with_columns(
    cell=pl.format(
        "{} ({})",
        pl.col("rate").round(2),
        pl.col("n").map_elements(lambda n: f"{n:,}", return_dtype=pl.String),
    )
)
order = (
    cells.group_by("dscr").agg(pl.col("dscr_order").min()).sort("dscr_order")["dscr"]
)
wide = (
    cells.pivot(on="ltv", index="dscr", values="cell")
    .with_columns(pl.col("dscr").cast(pl.Enum(order.to_list())))
    .sort("dscr")
    .select("dscr", "Below 55%", "55%–70%", "70% and above")
    .rename({"dscr": "DSCR \\ LTV"})
)
Markdown(viz.markdown_table(wide))
```

The effect is real but modest: even the worst cell is below 1%. The
monthly payment history is far stronger. Loans already 30 or more days
delinquent at the snapshot default within the year about half the time or
more (see the rating scale chapter). The model will need both: acquisition
underwriting to separate the large majority of current loans, and payment
history to identify the few in trouble.

Two limits from the data shape what the theory can deliver here. LTV and
DSCR are only known at acquisition (the data does not update property
values or income), so the model cannot follow either trigger over time
directly. And the DSCR definitions changed over time (see the data
exploration chapter), so DSCR must be made comparable across definitions
before it is used.

## Methods considered

```{python}
#| label: tbl-methods
#| tbl-cap: "Candidate methods."
methods = pl.DataFrame(
    {
        "Method": [
            "Expert scorecard / supervisory slotting",
            "Logistic regression on binned features (WoE scorecard)",
            "Logistic regression on continuous features (splines)",
            "Discrete-time hazard model",
            "Gradient-boosted trees",
            "Structural (option-pricing) model",
        ],
        "Merits": [
            "No data needed; transparent; the Basel slotting approach for income-producing real estate",
            "Industry standard; each bin's points are visible; handles missing values and non-linearity; robust with few defaults",
            "Uses all the information in each feature; smooth PDs",
            "Uses all of a loan's history; handles loans entering and leaving; standard for default timing",
            "Finds non-linear effects and interactions automatically; often the most accurate",
            "Grounded in the economics of the equity trigger",
        ],
        "Limitations": [
            "Not fit to outcomes, so PDs are hard to calibrate and validate",
            "Binning loses information and needs judgement; adjacent bins can jump",
            "Harder to explain and constrain; spline terms use up degrees of freedom",
            "Gives a hazard per period; a one-year PD needs a horizon and covariate path",
            "Hard to explain; can overfit with few defaults; less stable over time",
            "Needs property values and income over time, which the data lacks",
        ],
    }
)
Markdown(viz.markdown_table(methods))
```

Some notes on each:

- **Expert scorecards** are common for commercial real estate in banks,
  where defaults are rare. Basel's supervisory slotting criteria for
  income-producing real estate are an example: analysts grade a loan as
  strong, good, satisfactory or weak on the property's financial strength,
  the sponsor and the security package [@basel2]. Here the data is large
  enough to fit a statistical model, so slotting is a benchmark at most.
- **Logistic regression with weight-of-evidence (WoE) binning** is the
  standard credit scorecard [@siddiqi2017]. Each feature is cut into a few
  bins, each bin gets a score, and the PD is a logistic function of the
  summed scores. Bins also make it easy to impose a monotonic shape (for
  example, risk never falls as LTV rises), which keeps the model
  economically sensible.
- **Discrete-time hazard models** fit a logistic regression on loan-period
  observations [@shumway2001]. The annual snapshots built in the previous
  chapter are close to this design already, with a one-year period, so the
  logistic model *is* a discrete-time hazard model with a one-year step.
  The difference matters only if the model needs PDs over horizons longer
  than one year, which a rating scale does not.
- **Gradient boosting** builds an ensemble of small trees, each fit to the
  errors of the ones before [@friedman2001]. Benchmark studies find that
  ensembles often rank borrowers better than logistic regression, though
  the gap varies across datasets [@lessmann2015].
- **Structural models** value the default option from property value and
  income paths [@titman1989]. Without updated values or income, the model
  would rest on assumed paths rather than data.

## Chosen approach

**Champion: logistic regression on WoE-binned features**, fit with
statsmodels. It meets the requirements best: it is explainable bin by bin,
monotonic shapes can be imposed, the coefficients and their standard errors
are reported in a form validators and credit officers know, and it is
robust with fewer than a thousand defaults. Because the observations are annual
snapshots, the champion is a one-year discrete-time hazard model.

**Challenger: gradient-boosted trees** (scikit-learn's histogram gradient
boosting), fit to the same samples and features. It shows how much
accuracy the champion gives up for transparency. If the challenger ranks
much better, its partial-dependence plots point to the non-linear effects
or interactions the champion is missing.

**Benchmark: a simple expert-style score** using acquisition DSCR, LTV and
payment status, with no fitted weights. A statistical model that cannot
beat it is not worth its complexity.

### Calibration

The fitted model's PDs reflect the mix of years in the training sample. A
rating scale needs **through-the-cycle** PDs: the expected one-year default
rate over an economic cycle, not in the year the model was fit. After
fitting, the model's intercept will be shifted so that its average PD
equals a long-run default rate. A natural target is the average of the
annual default rates across all snapshot years, including the
out-of-time stress years: `{python} f"{yearly['rate'].mean():.2f}"`%
(`{python} f"{yearly['rate_ex_covid'].mean():.2f}"`% without the COVID
forbearance defaults). Which of the two to use is a Phase 4 decision, to be
reported with its effect on the grades.

### Delinquent loans

Loans that are already delinquent at the snapshot are rare but default at
very high rates. There are two ways to handle them: as a payment-status
feature inside the model, or as an **override rule** that puts every
delinquent loan in a high-risk grade regardless of the score. Banks often
use such rules. Phase 4 will compare both; the rule is simpler and keeps a
handful of delinquent loans from dominating the fit.

## How the choice will be tested

Phase 5 will test the champion against the challenger and the benchmark on
the test and out-of-time samples, for:

- **discrimination**: the area under the ROC curve (AUC), the Gini
  coefficient and the Kolmogorov–Smirnov statistic;
- **calibration**: predicted against observed default rates by grade and
  over time, with binomial tests [@bcbs_wp14];
- **stability**: the population stability index across years, and grade
  migration;
- **sensitivity**: how the PD moves with each input.

## Limitations of the approach

- **Binning is a judgement.** Bin edges affect the model. They will be
  chosen from the data with minimum bin sizes and a monotonicity
  requirement, and documented.
- **Logistic regression assumes additive effects** on the log-odds scale.
  The double-trigger theory implies an interaction between DSCR and LTV;
  the champion can include it only as a combined feature, and the
  challenger will show whether it matters.
- **Repeated observations.** Each loan contributes several snapshots, so
  standard errors from the logistic fit understate uncertainty. Standard
  errors clustered by loan will be reported.
